headline: Ward 32 pairs the highest income in Chicago with the least free time to enjoy it.
summary:
Every top mark in this ward comes back to the same fact, this is the most expensive corner of the city to live in. Median household income runs $166,248 a year, the highest of any ward, and the poverty rate sits at 5.9 percent, the lowest. The city's environmental-justice index scores the ward's population as the least at-risk in Chicago on the same kind of income, health and household data behind those two numbers. Even the nightlife number fits the pattern, 5.73 bars and taverns per 10,000 residents, the highest rate in the city, which is what a small, dense footprint full of paying customers produces when a ward's commercial strips get compressed into a few square miles instead of spread thin.

The weak marks price the same real estate a different way, through construction instead of dollars. Thirty-eight wrecking permits have gone out here, the most of any ward, and this year's news explains the pattern. A city commission cleared roughly $200 million in public funding for the Foundry Park project on the former Lincoln Yards site, and the City Council approved a 30-unit building on a lot in the ward that had sat vacant for years. Ground that gets torn down and rebuilt this often leaves less of it standing long enough to register as a landmark or sitting empty long enough to hold a garden, and Ward 32 counts zero of each, one rank off the bottom of the city on both. The social numbers run on a similar recipe. Weekly neighbor socializing and daily leisure time are both modeled from a ward's demographic mix and density, the same kind of inputs that produce the income and happiness numbers above, just run through a different formula and pointed the other way, worst in Chicago on both instead of best.
reading_the_rankings: Two of the flashiest firsts here need a second look before they mean what they seem to. Population vulnerability, ranked 1st, reads like a warning, but this measure runs in reverse, a lower raw score earns a better rank, and Ward 32's number one means the city's environmental-justice index found the least at-risk population profile of any ward, not the most. The modeled-happiness ranking needs the opposite kind of correction. It reads like an independent finding, residents here are the happiest in Chicago, but the model behind it is built from the ward's income, marital status, employment, homeownership and health mix, the same inputs already covered by the income and poverty numbers above, and the source itself grades the estimate low confidence. It is closer to a second reading of the ward's wealth than a survey of how anyone here actually feels.

news.headline: Ukrainian Village, Bucktown Apartment Proposals Approved By City Council
news.note: City Council approved a 30-unit apartment building at 1801-1809 N. Winnebago Ave. in Ward 32, on a lot the alderman's office said had sat vacant for years.

news.headline: Foundry Park In Line For $200 Million In Public Funding At Former Lincoln Yards Site
news.note: A city commission cleared the way for roughly $200 million in public infrastructure funding tied to the Foundry Park development on the former Lincoln Yards site, which sits in Ward 32.

news.headline: A Sliver Of Land Along The Kennedy Expressway Has Been Reborn As A Native Prairie
news.note: A Bucktown resident has spent years turning a strip of state highway land into a native plant garden, with the ward office backing efforts to keep it from being mowed.
